summary: Compares three approaches for configuring the address of an IPv6 recursive DNS server on a host: a Router Advertisement option, a DHCPv6 option, and well-known anycast addresses. It describes where each fits in ISP, enterprise, 3GPP, and unmanaged networks. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: To look up a name, your computer needs to know which phone book to ask. This compares three ways it can be told when it joins a network.

ra option vs dhcpv6 dns configuration
what are well-known anycast addresses for dns
subtitle: Three ways IPv6 hosts learn which DNS servers to use.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts need to know which recursive DNS server to use for name resolution, but there are multiple approaches with different trade-offs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three solutions: Router Advertisement (RA) options that include DNS info in router messages, DHCPv6 option for explicit DNS configuration, and well-known anycast addresses preconfigured in hosts.
tldr.outcome: Different networks choose different methods based on whether they need simple configuration, per-host customization, or minimal protocol overhead. The approaches can work together to provide fallback options.

facts.label: RDNSS option in RA
facts.value: Carries multiple server addresses with preference values

facts.label: DHCPv6 model
facts.value: Works with stateful or stateless configuration

today: RFC 4339 is Informational and describes the landscape of DNS configuration methods for IPv6 hosts as of 2006. It provides analysis and guidance but does not mandate a single approach. The three described methods are used in different contexts: RA-based configuration and DHCPv6 are both standardized and deployed, while well-known anycast addresses remain less common.

sections.title: The Problem: Finding DNS Servers
sections.content:
When an IPv6 host connects to a network, it needs to learn how to find a recursive DNS server (RDNSS) to translate names like example.com into IP addresses. The question is: what is the best way for the network to tell the host which DNS server to use?

IPv6 already has mechanisms for learning other network information, like the host's own address and the router's location. The RFC compares three different approaches to adding DNS configuration to these existing mechanisms, each with its own benefits and trade-offs.
sections.eli5: Your computer needs to know which address book to ask when looking up a name. Three different ways to tell it are described: through the router's announcement, through a special DHCP server, or by using a number everyone already knows.

sections.title: Router Advertisement (RA) Option
sections.content:
The RA option approach extends existing Neighbor Discovery (ND) messages that routers already send. A new ND option, the RDNSS option, carries one or more recursive DNS server addresses. When a host receives a Router Advertisement to learn its IPv6 address and default route, it can receive DNS server addresses at the same time.

The RDNSS option includes a preference value so hosts can select a primary DNS server among several, and a lifetime field that tells the host when to stop using that server and ask the router again. This is useful in mobile networks where DNS servers change frequently.

The approach requires routers to be configured with DNS server addresses, either manually or through DHCPv6 running on the router itself.
sections.eli5: The router already tells your computer its address and how to find the internet. With this approach, it also tells your computer which DNS server to use in the same message, all in one quick conversation.

sections.title: DHCPv6 Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option approach uses DHCPv6, a protocol designed for delivering network configuration information. DHCPv6 includes a "DNS Recursive Name Server" option that carries a list of IPv6 addresses of recursive DNS servers in order of preference.

This option works with both stateful DHCPv6 (where the server tracks which addresses are assigned to which clients) and stateless DHCPv6 (where the server only sends configuration information without managing address assignment). The latter is often preferred because it is lighter-weight.

DHCPv6 can deliver DNS information together with other configuration data, such as NTP servers or SIP servers. The DHCPv6 server can also send updated configuration later using a Reconfigure message, or by controlling when the client's lease expires, allowing the network to change DNS assignments dynamically.
sections.eli5: A special server dedicated to configuration (like a mailman) delivers your computer's DNS server address, plus any other settings it needs. This approach is more complex but gives the network more control over what each computer gets.

sections.title: Well-known Anycast Addresses
sections.content:
The well-known anycast addresses approach is simpler: instead of telling hosts about DNS servers, the network provides special anycast addresses that are preconfigured in every host. An anycast address is one shared by multiple servers; when a client sends a request to an anycast address, the routing system automatically directs it to the nearest server offering that address.

This approach requires no special protocol or message exchange. It avoids bandwidth overhead and latency, and it scales well because administrators only need to configure DNS servers as routers and the routing system handles the rest.

The downside is that routers must advertise the anycast addresses into the routing system, and administrators must manage route filters to prevent DNS queries from reaching outside their intended boundaries.
sections.eli5: Every computer is born knowing a magic address to send DNS questions to. The network makes sure that magic address reaches the nearest DNS server. It is the simplest approach but requires careful network setup.

sections.title: Choosing an Approach by Network Type
sections.content:
The RFC suggests different scenarios for different network types. In ISP networks, where many customers receive the same DNS configuration, the RA option is attractive because it adds no overhead; DHCPv6 also works well if the ISP already uses it for prefix delegation (assigning IPv6 address ranges to customer gateways).

In enterprise networks, where hosts may need different DNS servers based on their department or function, DHCPv6 is preferable because it allows per-host customization. Well-known anycast addresses can serve as a fallback.

In 3GPP mobile networks (cellular), the RA option is recommended because it requires the least overhead over radio links and allows configuration in a single round-trip. The protocol must work over the PDP Context connection between the device and the network gateway.

In unmanaged networks like homes, the choice depends on whether a gateway provides IPv6 and what the upstream ISP provides.
sections.eli5: Big cable companies might use the simplest router-based approach. Large offices might use the special server to give different employees different settings. Mobile phone networks prefer the lightest option since radio is expensive. Small networks do whatever works.

sections.title: Security and Interworking
sections.content:
All three approaches can work together. A host might first try to get DNS servers from a Router Advertisement; if the RA option is not present, it can fall back to DHCPv6. Well-known anycast addresses can be the final fallback when neither of the first two provide an answer.

From a security perspective, the RA option inherits the security properties of Neighbor Discovery. DHCPv6 can be vulnerable to rogue servers sending incorrect DNS addresses, but DHCP authentication (defined in RFC 3315) can prevent this. The well-known anycast approach has no protocol-specific security to breach, but denial-of-service attacks are easier because the addresses are known to everyone.

The RFC notes that full autoconfiguration and cryptographic security are mutually exclusive: in a zero-configuration scenario, the local network is assumed to be trusted. If cryptographic security is required, some secret information must be preconfigured.
sections.eli5: These three ways can all help each other: if one fails, another can take over. Each has mild security concerns, but if you trust your local network (which you usually must), they are acceptable.
